a: Comfort, comfort my people
p: The verbs are plural: God orders a group to comfort his people. Who they are is not said.
b: Nachamu is a plural command, so someone other than the prophet alone is addressed. The Targum says "prophets, prophesy comfort"; the Greek adds "priests" in 40:2. Many scholars, following Frank Moore Cross, hear the LORD speaking to his heavenly council, as in the throne room of 6:1–8 and 1 Kings 22:19–22: the plural voices of 40:3 and 40:6 would then be members of that court. Others think of the prophets as a group, or of anyone who hears. The doubled word is typical of these chapters (51:9, 17; 52:1, 11) and gives urgency. The verb is in the imperfect, "your God keeps saying", as if the order is repeated.

a: your God says
p: The covenant words return: the people Hosea named "Not my people" are "my people" once more.
b: The two short phrases echo the covenant promise "I will be your God, and you will be my people" (Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33). Hosea had named a child "Not my people", because "you are not my people, and I am not your God" (Hosea 1:9). Here, after the judgment of 39:5–7, God speaks of "my people" and calls himself "your God" in the same breath. The comfort begins with the relationship, before any change of circumstances is announced.

a: your God says.
p: Synagogues read 40:1–26 on Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after the Ninth of Av, the fast for the temple's fall.
b: The Ninth of Av mourns the destruction of both temples. On the Sabbath after it, called Shabbat Nachamu from this verse's first word, the reading from the prophets is 40:1–26. It opens the seven "haftarot of consolation", all from Isaiah 40–66, read on the Sabbaths between the fast and the New Year. Other parts of these chapters are read with the Torah portions: 40:27–41:16 with Lech Lecha (Genesis 12–17), 42:5–43:10 with Bereshit (Genesis 1–6) and 43:21–44:23 with Vayikra (Leviticus 1–5). For centuries Jewish readers have heard 40:1 as God's answer to their own mourning, not only to the exiles of Babylon.

a: Speak to the heart of Jerusalem
p: An idiom for speaking kindly, to reassure or win someone back: Joseph to his brothers, Boaz to Ruth.
b: Dibber 'al lev, "speak upon the heart", is used when someone speaks to win over or reassure: Shechem to Dinah (Genesis 34:3), Joseph to his frightened brothers (Genesis 50:21), the Levite to his wife (Judges 19:3), Boaz to Ruth (Ruth 2:13). In Hosea 2:14 God says he will lead Israel into the wilderness and "speak to her heart", like a husband winning back his wife. The picture here is the same: Jerusalem is a wife or a daughter who needs to be won back with kind words. The Plain keeps the image; the gloss gives the sense.

a: her term of service is over
p: Tsava' is army service or forced labor for a fixed time. Jerusalem has served her sentence.
b: Tsava' usually means an army, but it also means a soldier's term of duty or a period of hard, forced service: "Is not human life on earth a term of hard duty?" (Job 7:1; compare Job 14:14). The KJV's "warfare" keeps the military sense. The point is that the time is fixed and has now been completed: the verb male' is used of a term that has run its full length (Genesis 29:21). The Greek reads "her humiliation is fulfilled".

a: her guilt has been paid off
p: Nirtsah is a word of settled debt: the guilt has been accepted as paid, as in Leviticus 26.
b: The verb ratsah is used in Leviticus 26:41 and 26:43 of exiles who "make up for their guilt" in a foreign land, paying off what they owe as land pays off missed sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34). Here the passive form says the payment has been accepted. The word 'avon means both the wrong and the guilt it brings. So the comfort is not that the sin did not matter, but that its debt is settled. Christian readers often connect the verse with the servant who carries guilt in 53:5–6, 11.

a: twice over for all her sins
p: Kiflayim may mean double punishment, or the full equal measure, like a sheet folded in two.
b: Kiflayim is "double". Three readings are offered. Double punishment: Jerusalem has suffered twice what her sins earned (compare Jeremiah 16:18; 17:18), which is the reason for comfort now. The full amount: the root means to fold, so some take it as a matching copy, the punishment folded over to cover the sin exactly. Double blessing: a few read the line as the double portion of grace she will receive, as in 61:7, though the wording "for all her sins" suits punishment better. Most commentators take the first or second view.

a: In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!
p: In the Hebrew the wilderness is where the road is built; in the Greek and the Gospels it is where the voice calls.
b: The Masoretic accents join "in the wilderness" to the command: "In the wilderness clear the way", in parallel with "in the desert plain make straight". The Greek translator ran the words the other way, "a voice of one shouting in the wilderness", and the Gospels quote that form, which suits John the Baptist preaching in the wilderness of Judea (Mark 1:3–4). Both are possible Hebrew; the parallel lines favor the Masoretic division, and the Qumran community read it that way too (see the next note). Pannu derekh is "turn aside, clear away" obstacles from a road, as in 57:14 and 62:10.
orig: קוֹל קוֹרֵא בַּמִּדְבָּר פַּנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה (qol qore' bammidbar pannu derekh YHWH)

a: A voice calls out
t: The voice in the Gospels and at Qumran
p: All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist. The Qumran community used it to explain their life in the desert.
b: Mark opens his Gospel with it, joined to Malachi 3:1, under the heading "Just as it stands written in Isaiah the prophet" (Mark 1:2–3). Matthew and Luke follow (Matthew 3:3; Luke 3:4–6, where Luke carries the quotation on through the next two verses), and in John the Baptist says it of himself: "I am a voice of someone shouting in the wilderness, 'Make the Lord's road straight,' just as Isaiah the prophet said" (John 1:23). The Gospels follow the Greek, and they read "the Lord" as Jesus, whose way John prepares. More than a century earlier the Community Rule from Qumran (1QS 8:12–16) told its members to go into the wilderness "to prepare there the way" by studying the law of Moses, quoting this verse.

a: a highway for our God
p: Babylon had a paved Processional Way for its god. Isaiah's road leads God and his people home through the desert.
b: Mesillah is a built-up road. In Babylon the Processional Way, lined with glazed lions, carried the statue of Marduk through the Ishtar Gate at the New Year festival, and exiles may well have seen it. Isaiah's highway runs the other way: across the desert from Babylon to Zion, with the LORD himself coming at the head of his people (40:10–11; 52:12). The same road appears in 11:16, 35:8, 49:11, 57:14 and 62:10, and it recalls the exodus, when God led Israel through the wilderness.

a: Each valley will rise up
p: Kings had roads leveled before a royal visit. Luke quotes the lines, and Baruch reuses them for the return.
b: Ancient kings boasted of cutting roads through mountains, and towns prepared for a royal visit by smoothing the way. Here the whole landscape changes to make way for God. Luke quotes 40:3–5 in the Greek form, "What is crooked will become a straight road" (Luke 3:5), to describe John's preaching: hearts must be made ready. The Book of Baruch (deuterocanonical) reuses the image for Jerusalem's children coming home: God has ordered "every high mountain" to be made low and the valleys filled, "so that Israel may walk safely" (Baruch 5:7). Note the word 'aqov, "steep" or "crooked", the root of Jacob's name (compare 40:27).

a: Then the LORD's glory will be revealed
t: The glory that left and comes back
p: God's glory had led Israel out of Egypt; Ezekiel saw it leave Jerusalem. Now it returns, seen by everyone.
b: Kavod is the LORD's visible presence. It appeared in the cloud as Israel left Egypt (Exodus 16:10), filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the temple (1 Kings 8:11), and in Ezekiel's visions it left the temple before the city fell and returned from the east (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 43:2–5). Isaiah's promise goes further: "all flesh" will see it. The Greek adds that all flesh will see "the salvation of God", and Luke 3:6 quotes that (see the variant). John 1:14 says, of Jesus, "we have seen his glory".
r: Exodus 16:10; Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11; Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 43:2–5; Luke 3:6; John 1:14

a: all flesh
p: Basar means human beings in their weakness. The same words open the next verse: all flesh is grass.
b: Kol basar means all people, all living creatures, seen as frail bodies of meat and blood (Genesis 6:12; Psalm 65:2). The phrase links the two halves of the prologue: all flesh will see God's glory (40:5), but all flesh is grass (40:6). The comfort rests not on human strength but on God's word, which outlasts it (40:8). The Plain keeps "flesh" so that the link stays visible.

a: I answered
p: Read as "I answered", 40:6 is the only place the prophet of chapters 40–55 speaks of himself.
b: With the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek (see the variant), the speaker answers the voice in the first person. Many scholars hear here the call of the prophet of chapters 40–55, matching Isaiah's call in 6:1–8: a heavenly voice, a question, a commission. They see a new prophet, active among the exiles, who hesitates because the people have withered like grass. Readers who hold that one Isaiah wrote the whole book take it as Isaiah himself, or as a dramatic voice within his vision; the Masoretic vowels ("someone answered") leave the speaker unnamed. Either way the reply to the doubt comes in 40:8: the word of God will stand.

a: all its loyal love is like a wildflower
p: Hesed is loyalty or kindness. Human loyalty lasts no longer than a field flower. The Greek has "glory".
b: Hesed is the faithful love that keeps a covenant ("loyal love" on this site). Said of people, it is their loyalty or goodness, and it can be as short-lived as "a morning cloud" (Hosea 6:4). Some take it here as "beauty" or "charm", which fits the flower image, but the word nowhere else clearly means that. The Greek translator wrote "all the glory of man", and 1 Peter 1:24 quotes the Greek: "all its glory like the flower of grass". The contrast is between human faithfulness, which withers, and God's word, which stands.
orig: וְכָל־חַסְדּוֹ כְּצִיץ הַשָּׂדֶה (vekhol chasdo ketsits hassadeh)

a: for the LORD's wind has blown on it
p: Ruach is wind, breath and spirit. The hot desert east wind withers grass in a day.
b: Ruach YHWH can be "the Spirit of the LORD" (as in 11:2) or "the LORD's breath" or "wind". Here the picture is the scorching east wind from the desert, which dries up the spring grass in a few hours (Hosea 13:15; Psalm 103:16; Jonah 4:8). The Plain uses "wind" because of the image, but the same word stands in 40:13 ("the LORD's Spirit") and 42:1 ("my Spirit"): the breath that withers is also the Spirit that gives life (44:3).

a: but our God's word will stand forever
t: The word that stands, in 1 Peter
p: 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes 40:6–8 in the Greek and says the lasting word is the gospel preached to its readers.
b: The verse answers the prophet's doubt in 40:6. Yaqum means it will "stand up", be carried out, as in 14:24 and 46:10. The first letter of Peter quotes the Greek: "All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower drops off, but the word of the Lord remains forever." It adds, "This is the word that was announced to you as good news" (1 Peter 1:24–25), linking it to the "good news" of 40:9. Jesus says something similar of his own words (Matthew 24:35). James 1:10–11 uses the withering flower for the rich.

a: Zion, you messenger of good news!
t: Zion the messenger, or a messenger to Zion?
p: The Hebrew can make Zion the herald or name a herald sent to Zion. The feminine form slightly favors Zion.
b: Mevasseret Tsiyyon is "she who brings news, Zion". It can be read two ways. Zion is the herald: the city herself climbs a mountain and tells the towns of Judah, "Look, your God!" This suits the feminine participle and the following words to "the towns of Judah". The Plain follows it, as do the KJV and many modern scholars. A herald to Zion: a (female) messenger brings the news to Zion, as in 41:27 and 52:7, where the messenger comes to Zion. The Greek and the Targum take it so, and some modern versions put this reading in a footnote or the text. Either way, the message is the same.

a: Jerusalem, you messenger of good news!
p: Bisser, bring good news, became the Greek euangelizomai. From it comes the New Testament word "gospel".
b: Bisser is to bring news, usually good: of victory in battle (1 Samuel 31:9; 2 Samuel 18:19–20) or of a birth. The Greek translators used euangelizomai, and the noun euangelion became the Christian word for the message about Jesus, "the gospel" (Mark 1:1, 14–15). Isaiah 40–66 uses the word for the news that God has come to reign (40:9; 41:27; 52:7; 60:6; 61:1), and Jesus reads 61:1 in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18). Paul quotes 52:7 for the preachers of the gospel (Romans 10:15).

a: his arm ruling for him
p: God's arm is his power to rescue, the arm that brought Israel out of Egypt.
b: The "outstretched arm" is the LORD's strength shown at the exodus (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 26:8). In Isaiah 40–66 the arm returns again and again: it rules (40:10), carries the lambs (40:11), judges the peoples (51:5), is called to wake up as in the days of Egypt (51:9), is bared before the nations (52:10), and is finally revealed in the servant (53:1). Here the same arm that conquers also holds the lambs in the next verse.

a: he brings his reward with him
p: A victorious king brought home his spoils. God's spoils are his people. Revelation 22:12 echoes the line.
b: Sakhar and pe'ullah are wages, what a worker earns. A conquering king came home with plunder; here what God brings home, after his labor, is his rescued people, as the shepherd picture in 40:11 shows. Others read it as the reward God gives his faithful. The line returns almost word for word in 62:11, and Jesus says in Revelation: "I bring my reward with me" (Revelation 22:12), where the reward is repayment to each person for their deeds.

a: Like a shepherd he will graze his flock
p: Ancient kings were called shepherds. Here the strong conqueror of 40:10 carries lambs and goes slowly for the ewes.
b: Mesopotamian kings, Hammurabi among them, called themselves shepherds of their people, and the Bible gives the title to David (2 Samuel 5:2) and to God (Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1). The verse sets God's tenderness beside his strength in 40:10: the arm that rules gathers the lambs. Ezekiel 34 promises that God will shepherd his scattered flock himself, and Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). In 44:28 God will call Cyrus "my shepherd". Handel set this verse, with Matthew 11:28–29, in his Messiah.

a: in the fold of his robe
p: Cheq is the lap or the pocket formed by the robe at the chest, where a shepherd carried a newborn lamb.
b: Cheq is the bosom or lap: the fold of the outer garment above the belt. Shepherds carried weak lambs there, and Nathan's parable has a poor man's lamb that "lay in his lap" (2 Samuel 12:3). Moses complains that God expects him to carry Israel "the way a foster father carries a nursing baby" (Numbers 11:12): here God does it himself. Nahal, "guide", is used of leading a flock to water and rest (Psalm 23:2; 49:10).

a: Who has held the waters in his palm to measure them
p: 40:12–31 argues by questions. Job 38 and Proverbs 30:4 ask the same kind, and the answer is always God.
b: Scholars call 40:12–31 a "disputation": the prophet answers the exiles' complaint (40:27) with questions that leave only one answer. The style is the same as God's speech to Job, "Where were you when I founded the earth?" (Job 38:4), and Agur's "Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down?" (Proverbs 30:4). The measures are small and homely: a cupped hand, the span between thumb and little finger, a third of a measure, a merchant's scales. The whole world fits God's hand as grain fits a scoop. The point for the exiles: the God who handles the universe like this is not too small to save them.

a: Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit?
t: "The mind of the Lord" in Paul
p: Paul quotes the Greek, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?", twice: in Romans 11 and 1 Corinthians 2.
b: The verb tikken, "take the measure", is the same as in 40:12: no one can measure God's Spirit as God measures the heavens. The Greek translated ruach as nous, "mind": "Who knew the Lord's mind, and who became his adviser?" Paul quotes this form at the close of his argument about Israel and the nations, asking who ever knew the Lord's mind or became his counselor (Romans 11:34), and again in 1 Corinthians 2:16, where he adds that believers hold "Christ's mind". See the variant.

a: With whom did he talk it over, to gain insight?
p: In Babylon's creation story Marduk acts on the advice of the wise god Ea. Isaiah's God consults no one.
b: In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, recited at Babylon's New Year festival, the gods meet in council, and the wise god Ea advises; Marduk wins the kingship and makes the world. Marduk then plans the making of humans, and Ea, the wise counsellor, advises on how it is to be done and carries it out (tablet VI). R. N. Whybray argued that 40:13–14 deliberately denies any such heavenly adviser: the LORD has no Ea. Not every scholar sees a direct reply to the epic, and Israel's own picture of God's council (1 Kings 22:19–22; Jeremiah 23:18) shows the image itself was familiar. The verdict: the contrast with Babylonian belief is real and probably intended, whether or not the epic itself is in view. The words "justice", "knowledge" and "understanding" are the vocabulary of the wisdom schools (Proverbs 1:2–4).

a: The islands?
p: 'Iyyim are the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, the far west, and so the ends of the earth.
b: 'Iyyim (singular 'i) means land by the sea: coastlands and islands, especially the Mediterranean coasts and islands west of Israel, Cyprus, Crete and beyond (Genesis 10:5; Jeremiah 2:10). In Isaiah 40–66 the word stands for the farthest nations: they are summoned to court (41:1), they tremble (41:5), they wait for the servant's law (42:4), they are called to sing (42:10, 12) and to listen (49:1). The KJV has "isles", some modern versions "coastlands". The Plain uses "islands" throughout.

a: There is not enough in Lebanon to burn
t: All of Lebanon on the altar
p: Lebanon's cedar forests and wild animals were the richest the region knew. They would not make one fit offering.
b: Lebanon's mountains were famous for their cedar and cypress forests, cut for the temples and palaces of Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and for wildlife (2 Kings 14:9; Song of Songs 4:8). The verse imagines the forests as firewood and their animals as a burnt offering, and it says they would not be enough. The point is not against sacrifice as such but about scale: no offering can match God's greatness (compare 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 50:9–13; Micah 6:6–7).

a: He reckons them as mere nothing and emptiness
p: Tohu is the shapeless waste of Genesis 1:2. These chapters use it for the nations, rulers and idols.
b: Tohu is formless, empty waste: "The earth was shapeless and empty" (Genesis 1:2). Isaiah 40–55 uses it often: the nations are tohu (40:17), rulers are made tohu (40:23), idols are wind and tohu (41:29), their makers are tohu (44:9). Against this God did not create the earth to be tohu but to be lived in (45:18–19). The Plain renders it "emptiness" throughout, so the reader can trace it.

a: What likeness will you set up to match him?
p: Demut is the "likeness" of Genesis 1:26. Humans bear God's likeness; nothing can be made to show it.
b: Demut, "likeness", is the word of Genesis 1:26, where God makes humankind "in our likeness". Deuteronomy forbids making any likeness of God, because Israel "saw no form" at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:15–18). The question returns in 40:25 and 46:5, each time followed by mockery of idols. Paul makes the same argument to the Athenians: "we should not suppose that the Divine looks like gold or silver or stone" (Acts 17:29).

a: The idol is poured in metal by a craftsman.
p: Statues of gods had a wooden core, overlaid with gold or silver, and were set firm so they would not topple.
b: Most temple statues in Babylon were carved from wood and covered with gold leaf or plates of precious metal, then dressed and adorned; smaller figures were cast in bronze. Several craftsmen worked on one image. The chains may have held the statue upright or been ornaments. This is the first of several satires on idol-making in these chapters (41:6–7; 44:9–20; 46:1–7; compare Jeremiah 10:3–5, 9). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds a verb, "and makes", in this verse; it does not change the sense.

a: hammers gold over it
p: Raqa' is beating metal thin. God "hammered out" the earth with the same verb (42:5; 44:24).
b: Raqa' is to beat or stamp metal flat (Exodus 39:3; Numbers 16:39). Its noun is the raqia', the "dome" of the sky in Genesis 1:6, pictured as beaten out like a metal bowl. Isaiah uses the verb of God, who "hammered out the earth" (42:5; 44:24; compare Psalm 136:6). So the smith beats gold over a statue, and God beats out the whole earth. The Plain uses "hammer" in all three places.

a: Someone too poor for a gift like that
t: A poor man, or a kind of wood?
p: The Hebrew is unclear. Hamsukkan may mean "the one too poor", or name a hardwood known in Babylonian texts.
b: Read with the Masoretic vowels, hamsukkan terumah is "the one too poor for an offering": a man who cannot afford a gold idol buys good wood instead. But sakhan elsewhere means "be useful", and many scholars connect mesukkan with the Babylonian musukkannu, a prized hardwood (perhaps sissoo or mulberry) used for statues and furniture. Then the line says "As a gift, he chooses musukkannu wood, a tree that will not rot", and the verse is about the costly materials, not the poor. The Plain follows the traditional reading; the other is strong. The Great Isaiah Scroll differs in several small ways here but is no clearer.

a: Haven't you grasped how the earth was founded?
p: Literally "Haven't you understood the earth's foundations?" Creation itself should have taught them.
b: The Hebrew has no "since": "Have you not understood the foundations of the earth?" Some take it as "from the foundations", that is, from the beginning of time, in parallel with "from the very start". Either way the argument is from creation: the world's structure has told God's power since the beginning (Psalm 19:1; Job 38:4). Paul argues the same way in Romans 1:20. The four questions recall a teacher scolding pupils who should have learned their lesson.

a: the circle of the earth
t: "The circle of the earth": flat or round?
p: Chug means a circle or ring. It does not prove the Bible teaches a round globe, or a flat disk either.
b: Chug is a circle traced on a surface: the horizon line God "carved" on the deep (Proverbs 8:27), the vault or rim of the sky where he walks (Job 22:14), the boundary "traced" on the waters (Job 26:10). Some readers take the verse as proof that the Bible knew the earth was a sphere; others take it as proof that the Bible pictures a flat disk under a dome. Neither follows from the word. Hebrew had a word for a ball, dur (22:18), and it is not used here. The verse uses the view everyone saw: God enthroned above the round horizon, the people below small as insects, the sky over all like a tent. It is a picture of God's greatness, not a lesson in geography.

a: look like grasshoppers
p: The spies felt like grasshoppers beside giants. From God's throne, everyone looks that way.
b: The spies sent into Canaan reported, "In our own eyes we were like grasshoppers, and so we were in their eyes" (Numbers 13:33), and their fear kept Israel out of the land. Here the scale is reversed: from God's throne the whole human race, giants and empires included, looks like grasshoppers. For the exiles afraid of Babylon, it is the same lesson the spies failed to learn.

a: like a thin veil
p: Doq is fine cloth, thin as gauze. The heavens are spread out like the cloth of a tent.
b: Doq comes from a root meaning "thin, fine", the same as the "fine dust" (daq) of 40:15. The image is of light fabric stretched out, then fixed as a tent for God to live in. The psalmist says, "you spread out the heavens like a tent curtain" (Psalm 104:2), and Isaiah repeats the picture of God who "stretches out the heavens" (42:5; 44:24; 45:12; 51:13). It suggests ease: what is huge to us is a light cloth to him.

a: says the Holy One
p: Isaiah's favorite name for God appears here without "of Israel": the one who is utterly apart.
b: Isaiah calls God "the Holy One of Israel" about twenty-five times, more than all the rest of the Bible together, from the first chapter (1:4) to its last use (60:14), and it ties the book together (see the topic). Here alone in Isaiah the title stands on its own, "the Holy One", as in Job 6:10 and Habakkuk 3:3. Holiness here means God is unlike anything that can be compared with him: the question of 40:18 asked again in God's own voice.

a: Who created these?
p: Bara' has only God as its subject. Isaiah 40–55 uses it more than any other book except Genesis.
b: Bara' is the verb of Genesis 1:1, and in the Bible no one but God ever does it. Isaiah 40–55 uses it about sixteen times, for the stars (40:26), the ends of the earth (40:28), the desert's new trees (41:20), Israel (43:1, 7, 15), light and darkness, peace and calamity (45:7), and new things (48:7). The prophet joins creation and rescue: the God who made the world can make his people again.

a: The one who marches their army out by count
p: In Babylon the stars and planets were gods. Here they are an army God counts, names and calls out each night.
b: Babylon was famous for its astronomers, and its religion honored the heavenly bodies as gods: the moon god Sin, Shamash the sun, Ishtar the planet Venus, Marduk linked with Jupiter. Exiles living under that sky are told to look up and see not gods but troops: God leads them out "by count" each evening, like a general reviewing soldiers, and calls each by name, and not one fails to report. "He counts how many stars there are; / he calls each of them by a name" (Psalm 147:4). The verdict: the polemic against star worship is clear (compare 47:13; Deuteronomy 4:19).

a: my God has passed my case by
p: Mishpat here is the exiles' right, their legal claim. They feel God has stopped hearing their case.
b: Mishpat, usually "justice", here means a person's right or case before a judge. The exiles complain that their path is hidden from God and their case "passes by" him, unheard. Lamentations voices the same fear: "Why do you forget us forever?" (Lamentations 5:20), and Zion will say the same in this book (49:14). Notice that God's answer in 40:28–31 is not a promise of quick change but a reminder of who he is: the creator who never tires. Jacob and Israel are named together here for the first time in these chapters, and the pair recurs often through chapter 49.

a: The God of the ages is the LORD
p: 'Elohei 'olam: the God of long ages, past and future. Abraham called on El 'Olam at Beersheba.
b: 'Olam is a very long time, past or future: "forever" in 40:8. "The God of the ages" answers the exiles' sense that their present is all there is. Abraham "called on the name of the LORD, the eternal God" (El 'Olam) at Beersheba (Genesis 21:33), and Psalm 90:2 says, "from the ages past to the ages to come, you are God." The creator of "the far edges of the earth" also rules the ends of time.

a: He never tires, and he never wears out.
p: Two words, ya'af and yaga', run through 40:28–31 five times. God never tires; the idol-maker does (44:12).
b: Ya'af ("tire") and yaga' ("wear out") are repeated in 40:28, 29, 30 and 31, and the Plain renders them the same each time so the pattern shows. God never tires; young people do; those who wait for God will run and not wear out. In 44:12 the smith who makes an idol "tires" and has no strength. In 43:22–24 the second verb is turned around: Israel has been "worn out" with God, and has "worn him out" with sins. Compare Jesus' "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down" (Matthew 11:28).
orig: לֹא יִיעַף וְלֹא יִיגָע (lo' yi'af velo' yiga')

a: those who wait in hope for the LORD
p: Qavah is to wait with expectation, from a root for a stretched cord. It is the word of hope.
b: Qavah means to wait eagerly for someone (Psalm 130:5) and is related to tiqvah, "hope", and to qav, a measuring cord. It is not idle waiting: it is trust that keeps looking for God to act (8:17; 25:9; 49:23). The Greek has "those who wait patiently for God", and the Targum "those who hope for the salvation of the LORD". The promise is for exiles who are tired of waiting (40:27): the waiting itself is how strength comes.

a: will get fresh strength
p: Chalaf is to change or swap, as clothes are changed. Tired strength is traded for new.
b: Yachalifu koach is "they will change strength": the verb is used of changing clothes (Genesis 35:2) and of new shoots sprouting from a stump (Job 14:7). Old, spent strength is exchanged for new. The same phrase opens 41:1, where the nations are told to "get fresh strength" for their trial: the exiles who wait for God receive what the nations only pretend to have.

a: Like eagles, they will climb on their pinions.
p: Nesher is the eagle or griffon vulture. God carried Israel "on the wings of eagles" out of Egypt.
b: Nesher covers the great eagles and the griffon vulture, which can soar for hours on rising air without beating its wings (Micah 1:16 speaks of its bald head). At Sinai God said, "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me" (Exodus 19:4; compare Deuteronomy 32:11). The Hebrew may also mean "they will put out feathers like eagles", as the Greek reads, matching the old belief that eagles renewed themselves by molting: "like the eagle, you grow young again" (Psalm 103:5). The order is surprising: soaring, then running, then walking. Many readers see the hardest gift last: to keep walking without tiring.

a: Islands, be silent before me!
p: Chapters 41–45 stage court cases. The nations and their gods are summoned to prove they can foretell and act.
b: Since Begrich and Westermann, scholars have called passages like 41:1–5, 41:21–29, 43:8–13, 44:6–8 and 45:20–25 "trial speeches". The setting is a law court. The LORD summons the nations ("Islands, be silent"), invites their gods to present evidence, calls witnesses, and gives the verdict. The question is always the same: who has told the future and then made it happen? The gods are silent; Israel, though blind and deaf, is the LORD's witness (43:10). The courtroom form lets a tiny, defeated people hear their God judge the gods of their conquerors.

a: Let the peoples get fresh strength
p: The same words close 40:31. Many think they were copied here by mistake; others hear irony.
b: "Get fresh strength" (yachalifu koach) repeats 40:31 exactly. Some scholars think a scribe's eye picked it up from the line above and that the original said something like "let the peoples wait for me" (compare 51:5). Others keep it as deliberate: the nations are told to summon whatever strength they have for the contest, while 40:31 has just said where true strength comes from. The Greek has "for the rulers will renew strength", and the Great Isaiah Scroll agrees with the Hebrew.

a: Who has roused a man from the east
t: The man from the east: Cyrus or Abraham?
p: Most readers see Cyrus, named in 44:28. The Targum and Rashi saw Abraham, who came from the east and defeated kings.
b: The conqueror is not named until 44:28 and 45:1, where he is Cyrus the Persian, and most interpreters, ancient and modern, take him so here and in 41:25. Cyrus came "from the east" (Persia) and "from the north" (Media, 41:25), and in a few years beat the Medes (550 BC), Croesus of Lydia (547 or 546) and finally Babylon (539). The Targum and Rashi read it of Abraham, called from the east (Genesis 11:31) and victorious over four kings (Genesis 14:14–16), which suits the mention of Abraham in 41:8. Christian writers have occasionally applied it to Christ. The trial speech uses the conqueror as evidence: the LORD stirred him up, and the LORD said so in advance.

a: and calls him in righteousness to his service
p: In Isaiah 40–66 tsedeq often means God's saving action that puts things right: rescue, victory.
b: Tsedeq and tsedaqah are usually "righteousness", what is right. In Isaiah 40–66 they often name God's action to put things right for his people, and so "victory", "vindication" or "rescue" (41:10; 45:8; 46:13; 51:5–6). Here the Hebrew is literally "righteousness calls him to his foot": either God calls the conqueror rightly, for a right purpose, or "victory meets him at every step". The Plain keeps "righteousness" with God as the one calling. "To his foot" means to follow and serve, as in Judges 4:10. The KJV made it "the righteous man from the east", a line long read of Abraham (so the Targum) and, by some Christian writers, of Christ.

a: on a road his feet have never touched
p: Either the conqueror races along so fast his feet hardly touch the road, or he marches into lands he never trod.
b: The Hebrew is "a path with his feet he does not come". It may mean speed, the conqueror moving so fast that he scarcely touches the ground (compare the goat of Daniel 8:5), or new ground, lands he had never entered before. Herodotus tells how Cyrus reached Sardis before Croesus could gather his allies (Herodotus 1.79). The Greek has "the way of his feet will pass on in peace".
orig: אֹרַח בְּרַגְלָיו לֹא יָבוֹא ('orach beraglav lo' yavo')

a: I, the LORD, am first
p: God is first and with the last (41:4; 44:6; 48:12). Revelation gives the title to Jesus: "I am the First and the Last".
b: The claim answers the question "Who has done this?" God was there when the generations began and will be with the last of them. The title grows through these chapters: "I am first, and I am last" (44:6; 48:12). In Revelation the risen Jesus says to John, "Don't be afraid. I am the First and the Last" (Revelation 1:17; compare Revelation 2:8 and Revelation 22:13, where it stands beside "the Alpha and the Omega"). For Christian readers this means Jesus shares the identity of the one God of Isaiah; Jewish readers read it as a statement that God alone is eternal. See the topic page.

a: and with the last ones I am he
p: 'Ani hu', "I am he", is God's self-declaration in Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Its Greek, ego eimi, lies behind John's "I am".
b: 'Ani hu' is two words: "I (am) he." It means "I am the one", the same God through all time. It appears in Deuteronomy 32:39 ("Look now: I, only I, am he") and in Isaiah 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12; 52:6. The Greek translates it egō eimi, "I am". In John's Gospel Jesus says, "unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins" (John 8:24; compare John 8:28, 58), and "so that when it comes to pass you will believe that I am" (John 13:19), which echoes 43:10 closely. Christian readers see Jesus taking up God's own words. Jewish readers note that in Isaiah the phrase insists there is no other.

a: Be strong!
t: Everyone tells everyone to be strong
p: Chazaq, "be strong", runs through 41:6–13: the idol-makers strengthen each other, but God grips Israel's hand.
b: The root chazaq appears five times in a few lines. The frightened nations say "Be strong!" (41:6) and the craftsman "makes it strong" with nails (41:7): they must hold up the gods who are supposed to hold them up. Then God speaks to Israel: "I grasped you" (41:9, hechezaqtikha) and "grip your right hand" (41:13, machaziq). The irony is the point. In 46:1–4 the same contrast returns: the Babylonian gods must be carried, but the LORD carries his people.

a: saying of the soldering, "It is good."
t: "It is good": a jab at Genesis?
p: Claude's suggestion: the smith's verdict on his idol may mock God's verdict on creation in Genesis 1.
b: This is Claude's suggestion, not a settled view. In Genesis 1 God looks at what he has made and sees "that it was good" (Genesis 1:10, 12, 18). Here a smith inspects the soldering on a god and pronounces it "good" (tov hu'). The chapters around it argue constantly from creation (40:12–28; 42:5; 44:24), and the idol scenes in 40:19–20 and 44:9–20 parody the act of making. A craftsman approving his god's joints would be the creation story turned upside down: the creature making its creator. The words are common, so the echo may be accidental. Commentators usually read "It is good" simply as a craftsman's approval of the joint.

a: Israel, my servant
p: Here the servant is plainly Israel. The title will return for a figure with a mission to Israel (42:1; 49:1–6).
b: 'Eved, "servant" or "slave", was also a title of honor: Moses, David and the prophets are "the LORD's servant" (Numbers 12:7; 2 Samuel 7:5; 2 Kings 17:13). Isaiah 40–48 names Israel-Jacob as "my servant" again and again (41:8–9; 42:19; 43:10; 44:1–2, 21; 45:4; 48:20). In the songs that follow, the servant is sometimes Israel and sometimes a figure who has a mission to Israel (49:5–6). The Plain keeps "servant" in lower case so as not to decide who he is; the readings are gathered on the topic page. This is the first passage that names Israel so.

a: offspring of Abraham, who loved me
p: 'Ohavi means "the one who loves me": the source of Abraham's title "friend of God" (James 2:23).
b: 'Ohavi is a participle, "the one loving me": Abraham loved God. It is usually translated "my friend", as in 2 Chronicles 20:7, where Jehoshaphat prays about "the offspring of your friend Abraham". From these two verses comes the title "friend of God": James says Abraham was named the friend of God (James 2:23), and the Quran calls him Khalil Allah, "the friend of God". The Greek reads "whom I loved", turning it around. Abraham is named here because the exiles, like him, are called out from far away (41:9; compare 51:2).

a: I chose you, and I never rejected you
p: Exiles feared God had thrown them off. The answer is that his choice stands. Paul argues the same in Romans 11.
b: Ma'as, "reject", is the word of Jeremiah's fear: "Have you utterly rejected Judah?" (Jeremiah 14:19; Lamentations 5:22). The answer here is that God's choice of Jacob, made in Abraham, still holds after the exile. Paul asks the same question of his own day: "Has God rejected his people? Not at all!" (Romans 11:1–2), and he concludes that God does not take back his gifts or his call (Romans 11:29). How Christians understand that for the Jewish people today differs: see the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter.
r: Jeremiah 14:19; Jeremiah 33:24–26; Lamentations 5:22; Romans 11:1–2; Romans 11:29; Deuteronomy 7:6–8

a: Don't be afraid, because I am with you.
t: "Do not be afraid": an oracle of salvation
p: "Do not fear" opens a set form, perhaps once spoken by a priest to someone praying in distress.
b: Joachim Begrich proposed in 1934 that passages like 41:8–13, 41:14–16, 43:1–7 and 44:1–5 imitate a priest's reply to a lament: someone cries for help, and the priest answers with God's word telling the person not to be afraid (compare Lamentations 3:57). The pattern is: address, "Do not be afraid", the reason ("I am with you", "I have redeemed you") and the promise. Others find the background in prophecies to the kings of Assyria, where the goddess Ishtar of Arbela tells Esarhaddon not to fear. Either way, these chapters speak to the whole people as a priest or prophet once spoke to one person in trouble.

a: Don't keep glancing around
p: Tishta' is from sha'ah, look: to glance about anxiously, eyes darting for danger or help.
b: Tishta' is a rare form of sha'ah, "look, gaze". It pictures someone looking this way and that in alarm. The same verb returns in 41:23, where the gods are dared to do something so that "we stare at each other". The KJV's "be not dismayed" catches the feeling but not the picture. The Plain keeps the movement of the eyes.

a: with the right hand of my righteousness
p: God's "right hand of righteousness" is the hand that rescues and wins (see the note on 41:2).
b: The right hand is the hand of strength and of oath (Exodus 15:6; Psalm 98:1). "My righteousness" (tsidqi) is God's faithfulness in action, his rescuing victory (see the note on 41:2), so the phrase means the hand that saves and keeps its word. Psalm 48:10 says, "Your right hand is full of what is right." In 41:13 the image becomes personal: God takes Israel's right hand in his own.

a: Don't be afraid, Jacob, you worm
p: Tola'at is a grub or worm. God names Israel's weakness before he promises strength.
b: Tola'at is the worm that eats clothes and corpses (14:11; 66:24): the lowest of creatures. The psalmist cries, "But I am a worm and not a man" (Psalm 22:6), and Bildad calls humans "a worm" (Job 25:6). God does not deny Israel's weakness; he uses it as the starting point of the promise, and in 41:15 the worm becomes a threshing sledge that grinds mountains. "You small band" renders metei, "men", used of a people few in number (Genesis 34:30; Deuteronomy 4:27). Some scholars change the word to rimmat, "maggot" (as in Job 25:6), in parallel with "worm"; the Targum softens the line to "you tribes of Jacob".
orig: תּוֹלַעַת יַעֲקֹב מְתֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (tola'at ya'aqov metei yisra'el)

a: The Holy One of Israel is your redeemer
p: A go'el was the relative who bought a family member out of debt or slavery. God takes that role for Israel.
b: In Israel's law the go'el was the nearest male relative, bound to buy back land a poor relative had sold (Leviticus 25:25), to buy him out of slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49) and to avenge his blood; Boaz is Ruth's go'el (Ruth 2:20; 4:1–10). Isaiah is the book that calls God "your redeemer" most often, starting here (41:14; 43:14; 44:6, 24; 47:4; 48:17; 49:7, 26; 54:5, 8; 59:20; 60:16; 63:16). The title says that God treats the exiles as his own family and pays what it takes to get them back (43:3–4). The Plain uses "redeemer" for God, as on the rest of the site.

a: a threshing board
p: A heavy wooden board studded underneath with stones or iron, dragged over grain to break the stalks.
b: The morag was a sledge of planks, its underside set with sharp stones or iron teeth, pulled by oxen over sheaves on the threshing floor until stalks and husks were broken (2 Samuel 24:22; Amos 1:3, where it is a picture of cruelty). Such sledges were used in the Middle East into the 1900s. Here the worm of 41:14 becomes a brand-new one, and instead of grain it threshes mountains. Mountains here stand for the powers that hold Israel down (compare Micah 4:13).

a: The poor and the needy hunt for water.
p: God's answer recalls the exodus, when he gave water from the rock. Isaiah promises it for the road home.
b: In the wilderness the thirsty Israelites complained, and God gave them water from the rock (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:2–13; Psalm 78:15–16). Isaiah promises it again for the new exodus from Babylon: rivers on bare hills, springs in valleys, a forest of trees in the desert (41:18–19; 35:6–7; 43:19–20; 48:21; 49:10). The poor and the needy are the exiles, but the words also became a promise to anyone who thirsts (55:1; John 7:37).

a: the acacia, the myrtle and the olive
p: Seven kinds of tree are named. Several names are uncertain, so translations differ.
b: The cedar ('erez), acacia (shittah, the wood of the ark, Exodus 25:10) and myrtle (hadas) are secure. "Olive" renders 'ets shemen, "tree of oil", which may be the olive or a resin-bearing pine (compare Nehemiah 8:15, where it stands beside the olive). The last three are less sure: berosh is cypress or juniper, tidhar perhaps the plane tree or elm, te'ashur perhaps a cypress or box tree. The point is clear enough: trees that need water and good soil grow where there was only sand. Seven is the number of fullness.
orig: אֶרֶז שִׁטָּה וַהֲדַס וְעֵץ שָׁמֶן ... בְּרוֹשׁ תִּדְהָר וּתְאַשּׁוּר

a: says the King of Jacob
p: Only here is God called "the King of Jacob". Babylon's gods were kings; Israel's king is the LORD.
b: The title is unique, but the idea is not: Isaiah saw "the King, the LORD of Armies" (6:5), and God is "your king" and "the King of Israel" in 43:15 and 44:6. Babylon's New Year festival proclaimed Marduk king of the gods. A people without a human king (the last, Jehoiachin, was a prisoner in Babylon, 2 Kings 25:27–30) hears that its true king is calling the gods to court. Compare the news that Zion's God reigns (52:7).

a: The earlier things, what were they?
p: The trial turns on prediction: God foretold "earlier things" and they happened; now he announces "new things".
b: Ri'shonot, "the first, earlier things", and chadashot, "new things", are a pair in these chapters (41:22; 42:9; 43:9, 18–19; 46:9; 48:3–8). What the earlier things are is debated. Earlier prophecies already fulfilled, such as the fall of Assyria or the first victories of Cyrus; the events of Israel's past, from creation and the exodus to the exile; or prophecies of Isaiah of Jerusalem in chapters 1–39, which the later chapters see as fulfilled. The "new things" are the fall of Babylon, the return and beyond. The argument works the same way in each view: only the God who tells in advance and then acts is God. How long in advance is the heart of the authorship question (see chapter 44).

a: Go on, do something, good or harmful
p: An idiom: do anything at all. The gods are not even asked for help; any sign of life would do.
b: "Do good or do evil" means "do anything". Zephaniah's complacent people say, "The LORD will not do good, and he will not do harm" (Zephaniah 1:12), and Jeremiah says of idols, "do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do harm, and doing good is not in them either" (Jeremiah 10:5). The challenge is mocking: the LORD does not even ask the gods to save; any act at all would count as evidence. The last line has a Ketiv-Qere (see the variant).

a: Anyone who chooses you is abhorrent.
p: To'evah, "something abhorrent", is Deuteronomy's word for idols. Those who choose idols take on their nature.
b: To'evah is a thing God finds abhorrent; Deuteronomy uses it for idols and their worship (Deuteronomy 7:25–26; 27:15). Here the one who chooses an idol becomes to'evah himself. The thought appears also in the Psalms: "The ones who make them will end up like them, / everyone who trusts in them" (Psalm 115:8). The verb "choose" is the one God uses of Israel in 41:8–9: the LORD chose Israel; idol-worshipers choose nothing.

a: From the north I have roused a man
t: From the north and from the sunrise
p: Cyrus was king of Persia, to the east, and conquered Media, to the north, before turning on Babylon.
b: Cyrus II (reigned about 559–530 BC) was king of Anshan in Persia, east of Babylon. In 550 he took over the empire of the Medes, to the north, and he came down on Babylon from the north and east in 539. The Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian record, says his army entered Babylon without a battle, and the Cyrus Cylinder, his own proclamation, claims that Marduk chose him and called his name. Isaiah claims the same of the LORD. Jeremiah had already spoken of a destroyer of Babylon "from the north" (Jeremiah 50:3, 9, 41).

a: he will call on my name
t: Did Cyrus call on the LORD?
p: The Hebrew says he will call on God's name, yet Cyrus's own records honor Marduk. The line is read several ways.
b: "Call on my name" usually means to worship (Genesis 4:26; Psalm 116:4). But 45:4–5 says Cyrus does not know the LORD, and the Cyrus Cylinder credits Marduk with his victory. So the line is taken several ways. As written: Cyrus will invoke the LORD's name, as he does in the edict of Ezra 1:2, "the LORD, the God of the heavens, has given me" all the kingdoms. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "by his name" (bishmo): "he will call by his name" or "he will be called by his name", close to 45:3–4, where God calls Cyrus by name; some scholars prefer it (see the variant). The Greek: "they will be called by my name". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: deputies
p: Segen is a borrowed Babylonian title for a governor or official under the king.
b: Seganim comes from Babylonian shaknu, a provincial governor or official. Jeremiah 51:23, 28 and 57 use it of Babylon's officials, Ezekiel 23:6 of Assyria's, and Ezra and Nehemiah of local Persian officials, where the site renders it "deputies" too (Nehemiah 2:16). Cyrus will tread such officials like mud, as a potter works clay with his feet.

a: First, to Zion: "Look! There they are!"
p: The Hebrew of 41:27 is very short and unclear. Translators fill it out in different ways.
b: The Hebrew reads literally: "First to Zion, look, look at them, and to Jerusalem a messenger of good news I give." It has no verb in the first half. Most take it as "I was the first to say to Zion" (the LORD alone announced the news), with "Look, there they are!" pointing at the returning exiles or at the events now happening. The Greek reads "I will give Zion a beginning (or rule), and I will comfort Jerusalem", and some scholars emend the Hebrew. The "messenger of good news" (mevasser) links to 40:9 and 52:7.
orig: רִאשׁוֹן לְצִיּוֹן הִנֵּה הִנָּם (ri'shon letsiyyon hinneh hinnam)

a: Look at my servant!
p: Israel, an ideal Israel, the prophet, Cyrus, the Messiah, Jesus: each has been proposed for this first servant song.
b: Bernhard Duhm (1892) set apart four "servant songs" (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), and many now extend this one to 42:9. Who the servant is here is the oldest question about it. Israel: 41:8–9 has just called Israel "my servant ... whom I have chosen", and the Greek adds the names "Jacob" and "Israel" to this verse (see the variant); Rashi takes it so, and most earlier commentators, Ibn Ezra reports, took it of the righteous of Israel. An ideal or faithful Israel within the nation. The prophet himself: Ibn Ezra's own view, comparing 49:6. Cyrus, whom God also "calls" and grips by the hand (41:2; 45:1): Saadia Gaon's view, as Ibn Ezra reports it. The King Messiah: the Targum ("my servant, the Messiah"), Kimchi and Abarbanel, who rejects the readings of Cyrus, the prophet and the righteous of Israel. Jesus: Matthew 12:18–21 quotes the song of Jesus' quiet healing ministry, and the voice at his baptism echoes it. The topic page gathers the readings.

a: my soul is pleased with him
p: "In him I take delight": the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism seems to echo this verse with Psalm 2:7.
b: At Jesus' baptism the Spirit comes down on him and a voice says, "This is my Son, the one I love. In him I take delight" (Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22). Most scholars hear Psalm 2:7 ("You are my son") joined to this verse ("my chosen one ... I have placed my Spirit on him"). Matthew later quotes the whole song (Matthew 12:18–21) in a form close to the Hebrew in this verse: "Look, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, with whom my soul is delighted. I will put my Spirit on him." At the transfiguration Luke has "This is my Son, the Chosen One" (Luke 9:35).
r: Matthew 3:16–17; Mark 1:10–11; Luke 3:22; Luke 9:35; Matthew 12:18; Psalm 2:7

a: I have placed my Spirit on him
p: Like the shoot of Jesse (11:2) and the anointed messenger (61:1), the servant receives God's Spirit for his task.
b: In Israel the Spirit came on judges, kings and prophets for a task (Judges 3:10; 1 Samuel 16:13). Isaiah promises it to the shoot of Jesse (11:2), to the servant here, to the one anointed to bring good news (61:1) and to the whole people (44:3; 59:21). The perfect tense, "I have placed", says the gift is already given. Christian readers connect it with the Spirit coming down on Jesus at the Jordan, and Jesus reads 61:1 of himself at Nazareth (Luke 4:18).

a: He will bring justice out to the nations
p: Mishpat is justice, right order, God's verdict and way. The servant's task reaches past Israel to the world.
b: Mishpat appears three times in four verses (42:1, 3, 4). It is the decision of a judge, the right order of a society, and, as here, the LORD's way made known, close to "true religion" (compare 51:4, where "teaching" and "justice" go out to the peoples). The verb "bring out" (hotsi') is used of announcing a verdict. The servant is a judge and teacher for the nations, not a conqueror like Cyrus. The KJV's "judgment" is the older English for the same word.

a: He will not cry out. He will not lift his voice.
p: Unlike a herald or a conqueror, he does not shout. Matthew applies this to Jesus avoiding publicity.
b: Three negatives describe what the servant does not do. Readers have taken them in different ways: he is not a herald shouting proclamations, like the voice of 40:3 and 40:9; he does not shout orders like a conqueror (contrast 42:13, where the LORD himself shouts); he does not cry out in protest against his suffering (compare 53:7). Matthew quotes these lines when Jesus heals the crowds and orders them not to make him known (Matthew 12:15–19). The point in every reading is that the servant's power works quietly.

a: A reed that is crushed he will not snap.
t: The crushed reed and the dim wick
p: He does not finish off what is weak. Egypt was mocked as a crushed reed in Hezekiah's day.
b: A reed cracked at the stem is useless, and a flax wick that only smolders is about to go out. Ordinary people throw both away. The servant does not: the weak, the exiles, the nations near to giving up are kept alive. The Assyrian officer had mocked Egypt as "this crushed reed" (36:6; 2 Kings 18:21), the same two words. Matthew applies the line to Jesus' mercy to the sick (Matthew 12:20). In 43:17 the same words for a wick that goes out describe Egypt's army, drowned in the sea.

a: He will truly bring justice out.
p: Le'emet means "in truth, faithfully". Matthew has "until he leads justice on to victory".
b: Le'emet can mean "faithfully, reliably" or "according to truth", so that his justice is real and lasting. Matthew 12:20 has a different line, "until he leads justice on to victory", which runs 42:3b and 42:4a together; where Matthew's wording comes from is debated, since it matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek. The Hebrew is clear enough: the servant's justice will be true and lasting.

a: He will not burn dim, and he will not be crushed
p: The servant will not burn dim or be crushed: the same two verbs as the wick and the reed in 42:3.
b: The verbs repeat 42:3. The wick was "dim" (keheh); the servant "will not burn dim" (yikhheh). The reed was "crushed" (ratsuts); he "will not be crushed" (yaruts, from the same root). The wordplay suggests that the servant shares the weakness of those he helps but is not overcome by it, an idea that grows in 49:4, 50:6 and 53:3–5. English can carry it with the same words, so the Plain repeats them.
orig: לֹא יִכְהֶה וְלֹא יָרוּץ (lo' yikhheh velo' yaruts)

a: The islands are waiting for his teaching.
p: Torah is instruction, not only law code. The far nations wait for the servant's teaching. The Greek and Matthew differ.
b: Torah comes from yarah, "point the way, teach". In Isaiah it is the spoken instruction of God or a prophet, parallel to "the LORD's word": "For from Zion comes teaching" (2:3). The older English "law" (KJV) is not wrong, since the same word names the law of Moses, but here it is the servant's teaching, which the far-off islands long for. The Greek reads "and in his name nations will hope", and Matthew 12:21 follows the Greek (see the variant). For Matthew the nations' hope is in Jesus' name.

a: God, the LORD, says this.
p: Ha'el YHWH, "the God, the LORD", is a rare double title. A hymn to the creator introduces the call.
b: Ha'el, "the God", with the article, joined to the divine name, appears only a few times (Psalm 85:8). The titles that follow are a short creation hymn: he created the heavens, stretched them out, hammered out the earth (see the note on 40:19), and gives breath to everyone on it. The servant's call in 42:6 rests on this: the God who gives all people breath sends his servant to all people.
orig: כֹּה־אָמַר הָאֵל יְהוָה (koh amar ha'el YHWH)

a: He gives the people on it breath
p: Neshamah is the breath God blew into the first human. Here he gives it to every people on earth.
b: Neshamah is the word of Genesis 2:7: "Then the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground and blew into his nostrils the breath of life". "The people on it" is all humanity, not only Israel, and "spirit" (ruach) is life itself. Paul tells the Athenians the same: "It is he who gives life and breath and all things to everyone" (Acts 17:25), and he quotes their own poets to say we are his children. The creator of all people is the one who sends a light to them (42:6).

a: In righteousness I have called you
p: Most read 42:5–9 as God speaking to the servant of 42:1–4. Some hear Cyrus, whom God also calls and grips by the hand.
b: God now speaks to someone directly. The servant of 42:1–4, now addressed: most scholars and the church tradition. The task, a covenant and a light, matches 49:6 and 49:8, where it is the servant's. Cyrus: the words "called you in righteousness" and "I grip you by the hand" match what God says to Cyrus in 41:2 and 45:1, 13, and opening prison doors (42:7) suits a conqueror who frees captives (45:13). Israel, sent to the nations. Some think the passage once referred to Cyrus and was applied to the servant when the songs were joined to the book. On "righteousness" see the note on 41:2.

a: keep watch over you
p: Ve'etsorkha can come from natsar, "keep, guard", or yatsar, "form, shape". The scroll's spelling points to "keep".
b: The Masoretic vowels allow two roots. From natsar it means "I keep you, I guard you", as in 49:8, where the same form recurs. From yatsar it means "I form you", the verb of 43:1 and 44:2, 24 ("the one who shaped you"). The Great Isaiah Scroll spells it with a vowel letter (w'tswrkh), which fits natsar, and the Greek has "I will strengthen you", which decides neither. The Plain follows "keep watch over", which suits "I grip you by the hand".

a: a covenant of the people
p: Berit 'am is unclear. The servant embodies the covenant, for Israel or for all people.
b: Berit 'am, "a covenant of people", appears only here and in 49:8. If "people" is Israel, the servant restores the covenant between God and his people (49:8 speaks of restoring the land), while being a light to the nations. If it is humankind, as "the people on it" in 42:5, the servant makes a covenant for the whole race, in parallel with "a light to the nations". Either way, a person is called a covenant: the agreement is carried in someone. Christian readers think of the new covenant in Jesus' blood (Luke 22:20).

a: a light to the nations
p: Simeon greets the baby Jesus as "a light for revelation to the nations". Jewish thinkers have called Israel this light.
b: The phrase returns in 49:6, where the servant is to bring God's salvation "to the end of the earth", and the nations come to Zion's light in 60:3. In the temple Simeon takes the infant Jesus and praises God for a light that unveils God to the nations (Luke 2:32). Paul and Barnabas apply 49:6 to their own mission to the nations (Acts 13:47), and Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). In modern Jewish thought "a light to the nations" (or laggoyim) became a common way to speak of Israel's calling among the peoples.

a: to open blind eyes
p: Blindness and prison here may be exile and despair. The Gospels show Jesus doing this literally.
b: Blind eyes and prisoners sitting in the dark may be pictures: exiles who do not see God's hand (42:18–20) and are held in Babylon (42:22). Isaiah also promises literal healing (35:5) and freedom (61:1, where the Greek has "sight to the blind"). Jesus' answer to John the Baptist's question lists the blind seeing (Matthew 11:5), John 9 tells the healing of a man blind from birth, and Paul is sent "to open their eyes, so they turn back from darkness to light" (Acts 26:18).

a: I will not hand my glory to another
p: God shares his glory with no idol (48:11). Christians cite John 17:5; Jewish readers read a ban on any rival.
b: The verse closes the door on idols: no carved image may receive the praise that belongs to the LORD, and 48:11 repeats the line. It has also become part of the debate over Jesus. Christian readers point out that in John 17:5 Jesus prays for "the glory I had with you before the world existed" and conclude that the Son is not "another" but shares the one God's glory (see the note on 41:4). Jewish readers, and some groups that reject the Trinity, take the verse as ruling out worship of any being besides the one God.

a: Now I am telling of new things.
p: The new things "sprout" (tsamach), like plants. The same verb is used in 43:19 and 44:4.
b: God tells the news before it "sprouts". Tsamach is used of plants coming up (44:4), of new events (43:19) and of righteousness springing up (45:8; 61:11). Its noun tsemach, "branch, shoot", became a title for the coming king in Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8. On "earlier things" and "new things" see the note on 41:22.

a: Sing a new song to the LORD
p: The opening matches Psalm 96:1 and 98:1. A new act of God calls for a new song (Revelation 5:9).
b: The words match Psalm 96:1 and 98:1, "Sing a new song to the LORD", psalms that celebrate the LORD as king of all the earth. A "new song" is sung for a new act of rescue (Psalm 40:3; 144:9). Here it answers the "new things" just announced (42:9), and the whole world is invited: sea, islands, desert, the Arab towns and the mountain city of Sela. In Revelation the elders and the redeemed sing "a new song" to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9; 14:3).
r: Psalm 33:3; Psalm 96:1; Psalm 98:1; Psalm 149:1; Revelation 5:9; Revelation 14:3

a: you sailors on the sea, and everything in it
p: Yordei hayyam is "those who go down to the sea". Many scholars emend to "let the sea thunder", as in the psalms.
b: Yordei hayyam is "those who go down to the sea", seafarers (Psalm 107:23). But "and everything in it" (umlo'o) suits the sea better than sailors, and Psalm 96:11 has "let the sea thunder with everything that fills it" (compare Psalm 98:7). So many scholars read yir'am hayyam, "let the sea thunder", a change of a few letters. The Masoretic Text, the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek ("those who go down to the sea and sail on it") all have the sailors, and the Plain follows them.

a: the camps where Kedar lives
p: Kedar was an Arab people of the northern desert; Sela, "the Rock", a mountain stronghold in Edom.
b: Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13) and a powerful Arab tribe of the Syrian and north Arabian desert, known for flocks and tents (21:16–17; 60:7; Psalm 120:5). Sela, "the Rock", was an Edomite stronghold (2 Kings 14:7), perhaps near the later Petra. These are distant desert peoples, and their joy shows the reach of God's victory. Arabia was in the news: Babylon's last king, Nabonidus, spent about ten years at the oasis of Tema in north Arabia, as Babylonian texts record.

a: The LORD marches out like a champion fighter.
p: "The LORD is a man of war", sang Moses. Here the same warrior goes out to rescue his people from Babylon.
b: After the sea crossing Moses and Israel sang, "The LORD is a man of war. / The LORD is his name" (Exodus 15:3). The same phrase, "a man of war", returns here, as the LORD marches out again, this time for the new exodus. Gibbor is a warrior or hero, and the "battle cry" (teru'ah root) is the shout before an attack. The picture can seem harsh beside the quiet servant of 42:2, but the two belong together in these chapters: the LORD fights the powers, the servant brings justice gently.

a: Like a mother in labor I will moan
t: God as a woman in labor
p: Right after the warrior comes a mother giving birth. Isaiah uses bold feminine images for God.
b: After a long silence (the years of exile), God cries out like a woman in childbirth, gasping and panting. Next to the warrior of 42:13, the image is striking, and Isaiah uses others like it: God cannot forget Zion any more than a mother her nursing child (49:15), and God comforts like a mother (66:13; compare 45:10; 46:3–4). The groaning of labor suggests that something new is being born (compare 66:7–9), as Paul says creation "groans" in labor pains (Romans 8:22).

a: I will turn the rivers into islands
p: 'Iyyim are coastlands or dry land, so the rivers dry up. Some change one letter to read "dry places".
b: 'Iyyim, "islands" (see the note on 40:15), here means dry land: rivers dry up until only banks and sandbars are left. Some scholars read tsiyyim, "dry places", a small change. The drying of rivers is the reverse of 41:18, and it recalls the drying of the sea at the exodus (43:16; 44:27; 50:2).

a: Who is blind, if not my servant?
p: The servant who opens blind eyes (42:7) is followed by a servant who is himself blind: Israel as it is.
b: In 42:7 the servant is to open blind eyes; here the servant is blind and deaf. Most readers take this servant as Israel in exile, who saw God's acts but did not understand (42:20, 24–25), as Isaiah was told in 6:9–10. The contrast is one of the reasons scholars distinguish the servant of the songs from the servant Israel, or speak of an ideal servant and an actual one. The Greek reads "my servants" and "those who rule them", plural. Jesus' complaint to his disciples, "Having eyes, don't you see?", draws on the same idea (Mark 8:18).

a: the one made whole
p: Meshullam may mean "the one at peace with me", "the dedicated one", or "the one paid for". It is also a name.
b: Meshullam comes from shalem, "whole, at peace, repaid". Proposed senses: "the one in covenant (of peace) with me"; "the one dedicated" or "made perfect" (KJV "he that is perfect"); "the one paid for, redeemed". Meshullam was also a common name; a son of Zerubbabel had it (1 Chronicles 3:19), which has led a few to guess at a person behind the servant, a guess with little support. The parallel with "the LORD's servant" shows it is a title of honor, made sharp by "blind".

a: You see many things
p: The letters say "you have seen" (Ketiv); the margin reads "seeing" (Qere). The meaning hardly changes.
b: The written text (Ketiv) has ra'ita, "you have seen", which the Great Isaiah Scroll also has; the Masoretes' reading (Qere) is ra'ot, "seeing", an infinitive. Either way the charge is the same: Israel has seen much and heeded none of it. The verse moves from "you" to "he", as Hebrew poetry often does when speaking of and to the same person.

a: For his righteousness' sake
t: The rabbis' favorite verse on the commandments
p: The Mishnah quotes 42:21: God gave Israel many commandments to give them many chances to be righteous.
b: The verse says God, for his righteousness' sake, wanted to make his teaching great. At the end of the Mishnah tractate Makkot, Rabbi Hananiah ben Akashya says: "The Holy One wished to make Israel worthy; therefore he gave them much Torah and many commandments, as it is said, 'The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to make the Torah great and glorious'" (Mishnah Makkot 3:16). The saying is recited after each chapter of the Ethics of the Fathers (Pirkei Avot) in synagogue. "His righteousness" may be God's own, or, as the Mishnah takes it, the righteousness God wants for Israel. In context, the line contrasts God's great teaching with the people's refusal to listen to it (42:24). The Plain has "teaching" for torah, as elsewhere in Isaiah; the Mishnah hears in it the whole Torah.

a: Yet here is a people stripped and looted.
p: The picture is of a plundered nation. Babylonian tablets show many exiles farming and trading, not in jail.
b: Some exiles were literally imprisoned: King Jehoiachin sat in a Babylonian prison for 37 years (2 Kings 25:27–29), and the siege and deportations of 597–582 BC brought killing, looting and chains (Jeremiah 40:1). But cuneiform tablets from a village called Al-Yahudu ("Judahtown") near Babylon, from about 572 BC onward, show Judean families leasing land, paying taxes and doing business. The prison and pits here are therefore mainly pictures of a people captive, plundered and with "nobody to rescue" (compare Lamentations 1:3).

a: Wasn't it the LORD, the one we sinned against?
p: The prophet speaks as one of the guilty ("we"), then of them ("they"). The exile was God's judgment, not Babylon's win.
b: The answer to "Who handed Jacob over?" is not Babylon or its gods but the LORD: the exile was his judgment for disobedience, as Kings and the prophets explain (2 Kings 17:7–23; 24:3–4; Lamentations 1:18). The verse starts with "we" and goes on with "they", so the speaker counts himself among the sinners and also stands apart as the one explaining. For the exiles, this was hard comfort: if God sent the exile, God can end it (40:2).

a: and he gave it no thought
p: Jerusalem was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9). The worst grief in these lines is that Israel did not learn from it.
b: Nebuchadnezzar's commander burned the temple, the palace and every great house of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:9; Jeremiah 52:13). The verse says the fire blazed all around Israel and still Israel "did not know" and did not "set it on heart". The same phrase "set on heart" returns of Babylon in 47:7 and of the people in 57:1, 11. The chapter ends here, but the next verse answers it: "But now the LORD says this" (43:1).

a: the one who shaped you, Israel
p: Bara' and yatsar, "create" and "shape", are the words of Genesis 1 and 2. God made Israel as he made the first human.
b: Yatsar is the potter's word: "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7). With bara', "create" (see the note on 40:26), it describes God making Israel, probably at the exodus and Sinai, when a family of slaves became a people. The same words come back in 43:7, 21 and 44:2, 21, 24, and 45:9–11 turns them into the image of clay and potter. The point for exiles: the God who made them a people can make them again.

a: I called you by your name. You belong to me.
p: To name is to claim. God named the stars (40:26) and will name Cyrus (45:3); here he names Israel as his own.
b: Naming shows ownership and care: God calls the stars by name (40:26), calls Bezalel by name for his work (Exodus 31:2), and will call Cyrus by name (45:3–4). Here it is personal: "You are mine." Jesus uses the image of the shepherd who "calls out to his own sheep, each by name" (John 10:3). Many churches read 43:1–7 at baptisms and funerals.

a: If you cross the water, I am with you.
p: The sea and the Jordan at the exodus, and the furnace of Daniel 3: God goes through it with his people.
b: Water recalls the crossing of the sea (Exodus 14) and of the Jordan in flood (Joshua 3:15–17); fire recalls trials of every kind, and later readers thought of the three young men in Nebuchadnezzar's furnace, where a fourth figure walked with them (Daniel 3:25). The psalmist says, "We have been through the fire and the water, / but you brought us out to overflowing plenty" (Psalm 66:12). The promise is not that there will be no water or fire, but that God goes through them too.

a: I hand over Egypt as your ransom
t: Egypt, Cush and Seba as ransom
p: God pays a price for Israel's freedom: other nations. Cyrus's son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC.
b: Kofer is a ransom, the price paid to buy back a life (Exodus 21:30; Psalm 49:7). The picture is that God gives other nations to Persia in exchange for releasing Israel. Many historians note that Cyrus's son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC, and that Persian rule reached toward Cush (Nubia, south of Egypt). Seba was a people of Africa or south Arabia (Genesis 10:7; Psalm 72:10). Others take the line as a poetic way of saying "you are worth more to me than empires". The Greek has "Syene" (Aswan, on Egypt's southern border) for Seba. God is the redeemer who pays.

a: the one who saves you
p: Moshi'a, "the one who saves", is from the same root as yesha'yahu, Isaiah's name, and as Yeshua, Jesus.
b: Moshi'a is a participle of yasha', "save, rescue". It is a frequent title for God in these chapters (43:11; 45:15, 21; 49:26; 60:16; 63:8): "there is no one but me who saves" (43:11). The same root gives the prophet's name, Yesha'yahu, "the LORD saves", and the name Yeshua' (Joshua, Jesus), explained in Matthew 1:21: "he is the one who will save his people from their sins". The Plain uses lower case, as for "redeemer".

a: Since you are dear to me
p: Love, honor and preciousness: God gives the reason for his rescue. It is not Israel's merit but his love.
b: The verse uses three words: yaqar, "precious, costly"; nikhbad, "honored, weighty", from the root of "glory"; and 'ahavtikha, "I love you". Deuteronomy gives the same reason for the exodus: "It was because the LORD loved you, and because he kept the oath he swore to your ancestors" (Deuteronomy 7:8). Hosea says the same (Hosea 11:1). The exchange of "human beings in your place" is a strong way to say how much Israel is worth to God; it raises moral questions for modern readers, and commentators usually read it as poetry about value, not as a policy.

a: From the sunrise I will bring your offspring
p: By the 500s BC Judeans lived not only in Babylon but in Egypt and elsewhere. God promises to gather them all.
b: The promise names all four directions (43:5–6), as Deuteronomy had: "the LORD your God will gather you from there" (Deuteronomy 30:4). By this time Judeans lived in Babylonia, in Egypt (Jeremiah 43–44; later the colony at Elephantine) and in other lands. The gathering of the scattered people became a central Jewish hope, prayed for daily in the tenth blessing of the Amidah, "Sound the great horn for our freedom" (compare 27:13). Jesus speaks of many coming "from east and west" to the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:11).

a: my daughters from the end of the earth
p: God calls Israel's sons and daughters his own. Paul joins this verse to 2 Samuel 7:14: "sons and daughters".
b: It is rare in the Hebrew Bible for God to say "my daughters" (compare Deuteronomy 32:19). Paul seems to combine this verse with God's promise to David, "I will be a father to him" (2 Samuel 7:14), when he writes: "I will be your father, and you will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty" (2 Corinthians 6:18). The whole family is brought home.

a: all who bear my name
p: "Called by my name" means owned by God, as a field or a city is called by its owner's name.
b: Hanniqra' bishmi is "the one called by my name". To have a name "called over" something is to own it (2 Samuel 12:28): "Every people on earth will see that the LORD's name has been called over you" (Deuteronomy 28:10). The temple was the house "called by my name" (Jeremiah 7:10), and God's answer to Solomon speaks of "my people, over whom my name has been called" (2 Chronicles 7:14). Created "for my glory" means made to show God's glory.

a: You are my witnesses, the LORD declares
p: A famous rabbinic saying turns the verse around: when Israel bears witness, God is God in the world.
b: In the trial of 43:8–13 the nations' gods have no witnesses; the LORD calls Israel, blind and deaf as they are, to testify. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai drew a bold lesson: "'You are my witnesses, the LORD declares, and I am God': when you are my witnesses, I am God; and when you are not my witnesses, I am, as it were, not God" (Sifre Deuteronomy 346; also Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 12:6). The point is that God's reputation in the world depends on his people's witness. The verse also gave its name to Jehovah's Witnesses, who adopted the name in 1931 from 43:10–12.

a: and my servant, whom I chose
p: Most read "my servant" as Israel, the witness. The Targum has "my servant the Messiah"; the Greek adds "I am a witness".
b: The line can be read as two names for one group ("you are my witnesses, and my servant") or as two witnesses, the people and the servant. Israel, named "my servant whom I have chosen" in 41:8 and 44:1, is the usual reading. The Targum makes the servant an individual: "and my servant the Messiah, with whom I am pleased". The Greek has "Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I chose" (see the variant). Christian readers often think of Jesus, "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5), and of the apostles' charge, "You will be witnesses for me ... as far as the farthest end of the earth" (Acts 1:8).

a: No god was shaped before me
t: The strongest statement of one God
p: No god before, none after: 43:10–11 and 44:6–8 deny that any other god exists at all. How old is that belief?
b: These lines do more than forbid worshiping other gods (Exodus 20:3): they deny that any other god was ever "shaped" or will exist. With 44:6, 44:8, 45:5–7, 45:21–22 and 46:9 they are the clearest statements of monotheism in the Hebrew Bible. Scholars disagree about the history. Many, such as Mark Smith, hold that Israel's belief grew from honoring the LORD above other gods to denying the others' existence, and that Isaiah 40–48 shows that last step in the exile. Others, including most traditional readers, point to Deuteronomy 4:35, 39 and 32:39 and argue that the belief is older, and that Isaiah states it with new force against Babylon's gods. The verb "shaped" (notsar) mocks idols, which are always "shaped" by someone (44:9–10).

a: Since the first day
p: Gam miyyom is short and unclear: "from the first day", "from eternity" or "from today on".
b: The Hebrew is "also from a day I am he". It may mean "from the first day" of time (the Greek has "from the beginning"; the Vulgate "from the beginning"), with the KJV's "before the day was"; or "from today on", as some modern versions have it. The first fits the claim of 43:10 that no god was formed before the LORD. The Plain gives that reading.

a: For your sake I am sending to Babylon.
p: The first time chapters 40–55 name Babylon. It fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, by the Babylonian records without a fight.
b: Babylon is named here for the first time in chapters 40–55 (then 47:1; 48:14, 20). In October 539 BC, Cyrus's army defeated the Babylonians at Opis, and, according to the Nabonidus Chronicle, his general Ugbaru entered Babylon "without a battle"; Cyrus came a few weeks later and was welcomed. Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon tell a different story, of Cyrus diverting the Euphrates and taking the city during a festival (compare 44:27; Daniel 5). Babylon's fall opened the way home for the exiles (Ezra 1:1–4).

a: the Chaldeans, in the ships they used to cheer
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may describe Chaldeans fleeing in their boats, or their cheers turning to wailing.
b: Literally: "and I will bring down fugitives, all of them, and the Chaldeans, in the ships, their shout of joy." Berichim means "fugitives" (as in 15:5) or, with other vowels, "bars", the bolts of the city gates. The Chaldeans may be fleeing down the Euphrates in the boats they once celebrated, or, with a small change some scholars propose, their "shouting" turns into "laments" (reading 'oniyyot, "ships", as 'aniyyot, "mourning"). The Greek says "the Chaldeans will be bound in ships". The Plain gives the Masoretic sense. On "the Chaldeans" see the note at 13:19.

a: who opened a road in the sea
p: 43:16–17 retells the exodus: a path through the sea, Pharaoh's chariots lying dead. Then 43:18 says, forget it.
