b: The words recall Exodus 14–15: "The waters split apart" (Exodus 14:21), the chariots and horsemen drowned (Exodus 14:28; 15:4), and "Your road was in the sea" (Psalm 77:19). The participles describe God as "the one who opens a road", as if he always does it. Isaiah uses the exodus as a pattern for the return from Babylon (11:15–16; 51:10; 63:11–13), which is why 43:18–19 can say that the new will outshine the old.

a: like a wick they were put out
p: The same words as 42:3: the servant will not put out a dim wick, but Egypt's army went out like one.
b: Pishtah, "wick", and kavah, "be put out", are the words of 42:3, "A wick that burns dim he will not put out." Here they describe Pharaoh's army: they lay down, they did not get up, they went out like a wick. The servant spares the weak, and God snuffs out the oppressor. The chariots "lay down" (shakhav) like the dead, and "did not get up" is the language of death (26:14).

a: Stop calling the earlier things to mind.
p: Israel was commanded to remember the exodus. Here God says forget it, because the new act will outdo it.
b: Israel's faith rests on remembering: "remember the day you came out of the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 16:3). So the command to stop remembering is a shock. Most readers take it as comparison, not contempt: the new exodus will be so great that the old will fade beside it, as Jeremiah also says (Jeremiah 16:14–15; 23:7–8). Others take "the earlier things" as the disasters of the exile, which Israel should stop brooding over. In 46:9 God tells them to "remember the earlier things": both memory and newness matter.

a: Look at me, about to do something new.
p: The "new thing" is the return from exile. The New Testament hears it in the new creation in Christ.
b: "Something new" (chadashah) is the road home through the desert, with water for the people. The theme grows to "new heavens and a new earth" in 65:17 and 66:22. Paul writes, "if someone is in Christ, that is a new creation: the old things are gone, and look, new things have come into being" (2 Corinthians 5:17), and in Revelation the one on the throne says, "Look! I am making everything new!" (Revelation 21:5). Jewish readers have read the verse of the future redemption in the days of the Messiah.

a: jackals and ostriches
p: Tannim are jackals and benot ya'anah ostriches. The KJV has "dragons" and "owls"; the Greek "sirens".
b: Tannim (plural of tan) are jackals, animals of ruins and deserts (13:22; 34:13; 35:7). The KJV rendered it "dragons", confusing it with tannin, a sea monster (27:1). Benot ya'anah, "daughters of the ya'anah", are probably ostriches (KJV "owls"). The Greek translator wrote "sirens and daughters of ostriches" (strouthos is the ostrich here, as in 13:21 and 34:13), using the mythic singers of the Odyssey for the jackals. The desert animals, usually signs of desolation, now honor God because he has given them water.

a: They will recount my praise.
p: 1 Peter 2:9 quotes 43:20–21 in the Greek: a chosen race, a people for God's own, to tell his excellent deeds.
b: The Greek of 43:20–21 reads "my chosen race (genos), my people whom I acquired to tell my excellent deeds (aretas)". The first letter of Peter joins it to Exodus 19:6 to describe the church: "You, however, are a race that is chosen, a priesthood of kings, a holy nation, a people God has acquired, so that you may announce the great deeds of the one who called you out of the dark into his amazing light" (1 Peter 2:9). How the church relates to Israel's titles is a long debate (see the topic page on church and Israel).

a: Yet it was not me you called on, Jacob
p: God says Israel did not worship him. Before the exile they worshiped wrongly; in exile they could not sacrifice at all.
b: The emphasis falls on "me": "Not me did you call on." Before the exile: Israel offered sacrifices, but to other gods or with hearts far from God (1:11–15; Jeremiah 7:21–23), so in truth it was "not me" they honored. In exile: with no temple, no sacrifices could be brought, and God says he never demanded them as a burden (43:23); what wore him out was sin (43:24). Either way the passage moves from Israel's failure to God's free forgiveness in 43:25, "for my own sake".

a: Instead you made me slave over your sins
p: The verb is 'avad, "serve", the root of "servant". God did not make Israel slave; Israel made God slave over its sins.
b: In 43:23 God says, "I did not make you slave" (lo' he'evadtikha) over offerings; in 43:24 he says, "you made me slave" (he'evadtani) over your sins. The verb is the causative of 'avad, "serve, work as a slave", the root of 'eved, "servant". The same pair of verbs, "wear out" and "slave", recall Israel's slavery in Egypt (Exodus 1:13–14). The picture of God burdened like a slave with his people's sins prepares for the servant who "will carry their guilt" (53:11), a link Christian readers draw to Philippians 2:7, where Christ takes "the form of a slave".

a: sweet cane
p: Qanita qaneh: "you did not buy cane". Sweet cane was an expensive import for the holy oil and incense.
b: Lo' qanita li ... qaneh, "you did not buy me ... cane": the verb and the noun sound alike. Sweet cane (calamus, an aromatic reed) was one of the spices of the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), imported "from a distant land" (Jeremiah 6:20). Frankincense (43:23) came from south Arabia. The point is not that God wanted these luxuries; it is that Israel gave him neither costly gifts nor obedience, but sins.
orig: לֹא־קָנִיתָ לִּי בַכֶּסֶף קָנֶה (lo' qanita li vakkesef qaneh)

a: who wipes away your rebellions for my own sake
p: Machah is to wipe clean, like a dish or a written record. Forgiveness rests on God's own character, not Israel's merit.
b: Machah is to wipe clean (2 Kings 21:13) or to blot out writing from a record (Exodus 32:32–33). The psalmist prays, "As your compassion is great, / wipe out my rebellions" (Psalm 51:1). God says he forgives "for my own sake": not because Israel has earned it (43:22–24), but because of who he is (48:9, 11; Ezekiel 36:22). "Your sins I will not remember" is echoed in the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:34, quoted in Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17. When Jesus forgives a paralyzed man, his critics ask, "Who is able to forgive sins except the one God?" (Mark 2:7), a question this verse sharpens.
r: Psalm 51:1; Psalm 51:9; 44:22; 48:9; 48:11; Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12; Hebrews 10:17; Mark 2:7

a: Your very first father sinned
p: Jacob, Abraham or Adam? The line traces Israel's guilt back to its beginning.
b: Readers have named three. Jacob, the ancestor of "Jacob" the people, whom Hosea charges with deceit from the womb (Hosea 12:2–4; Genesis 27). Abraham, whose family "served other gods" beyond the River (Joshua 24:2), or who doubted God (Genesis 15:8; 17:17). Adam, the first human, a reading favored by many Christian interpreters who connect it with Romans 5:12. The "go-betweens" (melitsim, "interpreters", as in Genesis 42:23) are probably Israel's priests, prophets and leaders. The point is that Israel cannot plead innocence: its sin goes back to the start.

a: the leaders of the holy place
p: Sarei qodesh are the priests' leaders (1 Chronicles 24:5). Their holiness was taken away when the temple fell.
b: Sarei qodesh is the title given to priestly leaders in 1 Chronicles 24:5, "leaders of the holy place". God says he "made them unholy" ('achallel): with the temple burned, the priests could no longer serve and were treated as common. The Greek turns it around: "the rulers defiled my holy things". The verb form looks like a past tense ("so I made"), and most take the verse as looking back on the exile.

a: I handed Jacob over to the ban
p: Cherem was the total destruction devoted to God in holy war. Israel suffered what Jericho had.
b: Cherem is "the ban": what is devoted to God by destruction, as Jericho was (Joshua 6:17, "The town and everything in it are to be under the ban for the LORD"). The covenant warned that Israel itself could suffer this (Deuteronomy 13:15–17). The verse says the exile was that judgment. Yet the next verse begins "So now ... listen" (44:1): the ban is not the end.

a: Jeshurun
p: A pet name for Israel from Deuteronomy, from yashar, "upright". It may play against Jacob, "the crooked one".
b: Yeshurun appears only in Deuteronomy 32:15, 33:5, 33:26 and here. It seems to come from yashar, "straight, upright", and to be an affectionate name: "No one is like God, Jeshurun!" (Deuteronomy 33:26). In Deuteronomy 32:15 it is used with irony: "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked". Many hear a contrast with the name Jacob, linked to 'aqov, "crooked, deceitful" (compare 40:4; Jeremiah 17:9). God calls the people of crooked Jacob by the name of what they will be.

a: who shaped you from the womb
p: God formed Israel before birth, as he formed the servant (49:1, 5) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5).
b: The image of God shaping a child in the womb is used for a person called to a task: Jeremiah ("Before I shaped you in the womb I knew you", Jeremiah 1:5), the servant of 49:1, 5, and the psalmist (Psalm 139:13–15). Here it is the whole nation. The verse links the servant passages: Israel and the servant share the same vocabulary of calling from birth. The Greek adds "the beloved Israel" for Jeshurun.

a: On your children I will pour out my Spirit
p: Water on dry ground, the Spirit on Israel's children. Joel and Ezekiel promise the same; Acts 2 and John 7 take it up.
b: Rain on parched land is the picture of the Spirit given to the next generation, as in 32:15, where the Spirit "is poured out from on high" and the desert becomes an orchard. Ezekiel promises God's Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26–27; 39:29), and Joel promises that God will pour out his spirit "on all flesh" (Joel 2:28). At Pentecost Peter quotes Joel (Acts 2:17), and in John 7:37–39 Jesus promises rivers of living water, "about the Spirit". Many churches connect the water and Spirit with baptism (John 3:5).

a: They will spring up in the middle of the grass
p: The Hebrew "among grass" is odd. The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek read it slightly differently.
b: The Masoretic Text has bevein chatsir, "in between grass". The Great Isaiah Scroll reads kevein, "as in between", and the Greek "like grass in the middle of water". Some scholars read the first word as a kind of tree, "like a tamarisk", to match the poplars. The meaning is clear: Israel's children will shoot up fast and green. On "spring up" (tsamach) see the note on 42:9.

a: Another will write on his hand
t: A name written on the hand
p: Slaves and devotees could be marked on the hand with an owner's or a god's name. Here people mark themselves the LORD's.
b: In the ancient world slaves were sometimes marked on the hand or wrist with the owner's name, and temple servants with the name of their god; papyri from Elephantine in Egypt describe slaves marked this way. Here it is not clear whether the writing is in ink or a tattoo, or whether the Hebrew means "will write with his hand". Leviticus 19:28 says, "do not put tattooed writing on yourselves", so a permanent mark would have been striking. Ezekiel 9:4 has a mark on the forehead for the faithful, and Revelation the names of God and the Lamb on the foreheads of the redeemed (Revelation 7:3; 14:1), opposite the beast's "mark on their right hand or on their forehead" (Revelation 13:16).

a: This one will say, "I am the LORD's."
p: Israelites renewing their loyalty, or foreigners joining Israel? Readers have taken the verse both ways.
b: Israelites: the "children" of 44:3, the new generation, gladly claim the names Jacob and Israel that their parents had shamed. Foreigners: people of other nations join the LORD's people and take Israel's name as a title of honor, as 56:3–8 promises and as Psalm 87:4–6 imagines of Zion. The Mekhilta (on Exodus 22:20), and Rashi after it, find four groups in the four clauses: the wholly righteous, the children of the wicked who died young, those who repent, and converts who take Israel's name. Christian readers have seen in it the nations joining God's people. Both may be meant: the outpouring of the Spirit makes people want to belong.

a: I am first, and I am last
t: "I am the First and the Last"
p: Revelation gives this title, spoken here by the LORD, to the risen Jesus (Revelation 1:17; 2:8; 22:13).
b: God has said it in shorter form in 41:4 and will say it again in 48:12. The Greek here has "I am first and I am after these things", so Revelation's "the Last" follows the Hebrew rather than the Greek of this verse. In Revelation the risen Jesus tells John, "Don't be afraid. I am the First and the Last" (Revelation 1:17), and to the church in Smyrna he is "the First and the Last" who died and came back to life (Revelation 2:8). In Revelation 22:13 he joins it with "the Alpha and the Omega" and "the Beginning and the End". Because 44:6 adds "except for me there is no god", the title in Revelation is one of the New Testament's strongest ways of placing Jesus with the one God. Churches differ on what this means (see the card on this chapter).

a: the LORD of Armies
p: King, redeemer, LORD of Armies: three titles before God speaks. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds "is his name".
b: The verse piles up titles: "the King of Israel", "its redeemer" (see the note on 41:14) and "the LORD of Armies" (on that title see the note at its first use in the book). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "the LORD of Armies is his name", as in 47:4 and 48:2; the difference is small. The Greek has "the God of armies" and lacks the name.

a: from the time I set up a people of long ago
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may be Israel, chosen long ago, or humankind; some scholars emend the line.
b: Missumi 'am 'olam is "since my setting an ancient people". It may mean Israel, God's people from of old, whose story God has told from the start; or humanity in general, as the Greek has it, "since I made man forever". Many scholars emend slightly to "Who announced from of old the things to come?", which fits the next lines. The sense of the challenge is clear either way: let any rival give a full account of history from the beginning and tell the future.

a: No, there is no rock. I know none.
p: Tsur, "rock", is a title for God in the Song of Moses and the Psalms: steady, a place of safety.
b: Tsur is a rock cliff, a place to hide and stand firm. Moses' song calls God "the Rock" (Deuteronomy 32:4, "He is the Rock"), Hannah prays, "There is no rock like our God" (1 Samuel 2:2), and David asks, "Who is a rock, if not our God?" (Psalm 18:31). Isaiah used it in 17:10, 26:4 and 30:29. God's "I know none" is a striking way to say there is no other: even God knows of no other god. Paul says the rock in the wilderness "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).
orig: וְאֵין צוּר בַּל־יָדָעְתִּי (ve'ein tsur bal yada'ti)

a: Those who shape idols, every one of them, are emptiness
t: The idol satire: poem or prose, fair or unfair?
p: 44:9–20 mocks the idol-maker in detail. Many think it was added; many ask whether it is fair to idol-worshipers.
b: Form: Westermann and others think 44:9–20 is a prose piece placed into the poems; others set it as rough verse, and the Plain does, because its lines move in parallel pairs. It interrupts 44:8 and 44:21, which fit together, but similar satires appear in 40:19–20, 41:6–7 and 46:5–7. Fairness: Babylonian worshipers did not think the wood was the god. A statue became the god's dwelling through rites that "opened its mouth" and washed it (see the note on 44:13). The satire ignores that on purpose: from Israel's view, a god who needs to be made, fixed and carried is no god at all. Jeremiah 10:1–16, Psalm 115:4–8 and the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19 use the same argument.

a: Their own witnesses see nothing and know nothing
p: In the Masoretic Text the word "they" (hemmah) in this line carries dots, a scribal sign of doubt.
b: The Masoretes placed special dots over hemmah, "they", in this line: it is one of the fifteen "extraordinary points" (puncta extraordinaria) of the Hebrew Bible, ten of them in the Torah. Such dots probably mark a word the scribes doubted, perhaps one missing from some manuscripts. Without it the line reads "and their witnesses do not see". The witnesses are the idols themselves, or their worshipers, who are as blind as the images (compare Psalm 115:8). The meaning does not change.

a: He has drunk no water, and he tires.
p: The smith "tires" (ya'af), the verb of 40:28–31. God never tires; the man who makes a god does.
b: Vayi'af, "and he tires", is the verb of 40:28, "He never tires", and of 40:31, "They will walk and not tire". The smith works so hard on his god that he forgets to eat and drink and wears himself out. The satire turns on this: the maker of a god has less strength than the God who made him and gives strength to the tired (40:29).
orig: לֹא־שָׁתָה מַיִם וַיִּיעָף (lo' shatah mayim vayi'af)

a: the good looks of a human being
p: God made humans in his image; here a human makes a god in his own. Paul draws the same contrast in Romans 1.
b: "So God created the human in his image" (Genesis 1:27). The carpenter reverses it: he gives his god "the form of a man" (tavnit 'ish) and human beauty (tif'eret 'adam). Paul says people traded "the glory of the God who does not decay" for the likeness of a decaying human (Romans 1:23). The idol is placed in a house, a temple or a household shrine.

a: to stay in a house
t: How a statue became a god in Babylon
p: In Babylon, rituals "washed" and "opened the mouth" of a new statue so the god could live in it.
b: Mesopotamian texts describe the mis pi ("washing of the mouth") and pit pi ("opening of the mouth") rituals. After craftsmen finished a statue, priests performed a long ceremony, ritually cut off the craftsmen's hands with a wooden sword, and declared that the gods, not humans, had made it. Only then was the statue taken into its temple, its "house", as the dwelling of the god. Isaiah's satire describes exactly the human work the ritual tried to deny. The verdict: the parallel is real and well documented, and the prophet's mockery aims at the heart of the belief.

a: He plants a pine, and the rain makes it big.
p: The carver plants the tree, but God sends the rain that grows it. Several tree names are uncertain.
b: The man plants an 'oren (pine, laurel or ash) and waits for rain. The rain is God's (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 14:22), so even the wood of the idol comes from the LORD's gift. The Greek makes this plain: he cut "wood from the forest, which the Lord planted". The other trees, tirzah (perhaps the holm oak) and 'allon (oak), are not certain.
orig: נָטַע אֹרֶן וְגֶשֶׁם יְגַדֵּל (nata' 'oren vegeshem yegaddel)

a: Rescue me! You are my god.
t: Prayer to a block of wood
p: The worshiper prays to the leftover wood the prayer Israel prays to God. Jeremiah and Wisdom tell the same story.
b: "Rescue me" (hatsileni) is the cry of the psalms to the LORD (Psalm 31:2; 59:1). Here it goes to a log, half of which has just cooked supper. The deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon retells the scene: a woodcutter burns the scraps, carves the rest into an image, sets it in a niche, fastens it with iron so it will not fall, and prays to it for health and life (Wisdom of Solomon 13:11–19). Psalm 115 says, "Their idols are silver and gold, / something human hands have made." Compare also Deuteronomy 4:28 and the Letter of Jeremiah.
r: Psalm 31:2; Psalm 115:4–8; Wisdom of Solomon 13:11–19; Letter of Jeremiah; Deuteronomy 4:28; Jeremiah 10:3–5

a: Their eyes are smeared shut
p: Tach is to coat or plaster. Who blinded them is not said. Isaiah's call spoke of eyes made blind (6:10).
b: Tach is the verb for plastering a wall (Leviticus 14:42; Ezekiel 13:10–15). Their eyes are coated so they cannot see. The Hebrew does not name the subject: the Greek has a passive, and some versions supply "he" (God), recalling 6:9–10, where the prophet is told to make the people's eyes blind. The idol-makers become like their idols, of which Psalm 115:5 says, "eyes they have, but they cannot see" (compare 44:9).
orig: כִּי טַח מֵרְאוֹת עֵינֵיהֶם (ki tach mer'ot 'eineihem)

a: He grazes on ashes.
p: Ro'eh 'efer is "he feeds on ashes": the worshiper lives on the leftovers of his own fire.
b: Ro'eh means "pasturing, grazing", and so "shepherd". The idol-worshiper feeds on ashes, the leftovers of the fire he cooked with: what nourishes him is worthless (compare Hosea 12:1, "Ephraim grazes on wind"). The next line explains how: "A heart that has been fooled has turned him aside." He is not only wrong but deceived, so he cannot see the lie in his own hand. On a possible link with "my shepherd" in 44:28, see the shepherd topic.

a: This thing in my right hand is a lie, isn't it?
p: Sheqer is a lie, a fraud. Paul says idolaters traded God's truth for a lie.
b: The idol is sheqer, "a lie", a thing that pretends to be what it is not (Jeremiah 10:14; 16:19). The worshiper holds it in his right hand, the hand of strength, and cannot see what it is. Paul uses the same idea in Romans 1:25: they traded God's truth for the lie, and revered and served what was made instead of the one who made it.

a: Israel, you will not be forgotten by me.
p: The Hebrew form is rare: "you will not be forgotten by me". The Greek reads "do not forget me".
b: Lo' tinnasheni is an unusual passive with an object ending: "you will not be forgotten by me". The Greek reads "do not forget me"; the Great Isaiah Scroll has tish'eni, which may mean the same or "do not deceive me" (see the variant). In context God has just told Israel to "keep these things in mind", so either reading fits: Israel must not forget God, and God will not forget Israel (49:15).

a: Like a thick cloud I have wiped away your rebellions
t: Forgiven first, then called to return
p: God has already wiped out the sins, then says "Turn back to me". Forgiveness comes before repentance here.
b: The sins vanish like morning cloud burned off by the sun (compare Hosea 6:4; 13:3). The order is striking: "I have wiped away ... Turn back to me. I have redeemed you." The call to return (shuv, the word for repentance) rests on what God has already done. Christian readers, especially in the Protestant traditions, often cite the verse for grace that comes before repentance. Jewish teaching on teshuvah (repentance) also reads it as God's invitation, and the rabbis linked it with "Return, Israel" (Hosea 14:1). Both see the return as the human answer to God's forgiving act.

a: Shout, you depths under the earth!
p: Heavens, earth's depths, mountains and forest are called to sing. The psalms and Paul's "creation waits" echo it.
b: Tachtiyyot 'arets, "the lowest parts of the earth", is the deep below, even the world of the dead (Psalm 63:9); the psalmist speaks of being "embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth" (Psalm 139:15). Here everything from heaven to the depths joins in, as in 49:13 and 55:12 and in Psalm 96:12, "then all the forest trees will shout for joy". Paul says creation waits eagerly for God's children to be revealed (Romans 8:19–22). Ephesians 4:9 uses "the lower parts of the earth" of Christ's descent.

a: who stretched out the heavens alone
p: "Alone he spreads out the skies", says Job. No one helped God make the world, and no one helps him save Israel.
b: Job says of God, "Alone he spreads out the skies / and tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8). Isaiah stresses the same "alone" (levaddi) because the next verses turn to history: the God who made the world without help also overturns diviners and raises up Cyrus. In the Babylonian creation story Marduk acts with the gods' council behind him (see the note on 40:14). The last words of the line are a Ketiv-Qere (see the variant).

a: who wrecks the omens of the babblers
p: Babylon's priests read the future from livers, stars and dreams. God says their signs will fail.
b: Babylon was the center of ancient divination. Its experts read the future from the livers of sacrificed sheep, the movements of stars and planets, oil on water and dreams; libraries held omen collections such as Enuma Anu Enlil, with thousands of signs. Baddim, "babblers" or "empty talkers", is used of Babylon's diviners in Jeremiah 50:36. The book mocks Babylon's astrologers again in 47:12–13, and Daniel's Babylonian court has its magicians and Chaldeans (Daniel 2:2). Here the God who foretold Cyrus shows up the foretellers.

a: who makes his servant's word stand
p: "His servant" is the one whose word comes true: Isaiah, the prophets, or Israel.
b: The parallel line has "his messengers", so the servant is probably a prophet. Isaiah himself, called "my servant" in 20:3, whose earlier words about Babylon (13–14; 21; 39:6–7) now come true. The prophets in general, whose message God carries out. Israel, the servant of 44:21, whose witness is confirmed. The Greek reads "his servant" (pais), the word it uses for Israel in 44:21. In each case the point is the trial's: God's word is shown true by events, the diviners' is not.

a: and of the towns of Judah
p: Babylon left Jerusalem and many towns of Judah in ruins (586 BC). The rebuilding began slowly after 538.
b: Archaeology shows widespread destruction in Judah in the Babylonian campaigns of 588–586 BC: Lachish, Arad, Ramat Rahel, Jerusalem's walls and houses. Lamentations describes the ruined city (Lamentations 1:1–4). After Cyrus's decree some exiles returned (Ezra 1–2), and the lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 and 11 name towns resettled. The rebuilding was slow: in Nehemiah's day, about 445 BC, Jerusalem's wall was still "breached" (Nehemiah 1:3).

a: who says to the deep, "Dry up!
p: The deep recalls the sea of the exodus and the waters of creation. Greek historians say Cyrus drained the Euphrates.
b: Tsulah is "the depth" of the sea (Jonah 2:3), and drying it recalls the exodus (51:10; Exodus 15:8). In Babylonian myth Marduk split the sea-monster Tiamat to make the world, and the Bible sometimes uses that kind of language for God's power over the sea (51:9–10). Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.5) say Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates and marching in along the riverbed, and Jeremiah 50:38 and 51:36 speak of Babylon's waters drying up. The Babylonian records say the city fell without a battle, so the Greek story may be later legend. The verdict: the verse is first an exodus image; a link to the Euphrates is possible, not certain.

a: who says of Cyrus
p: The prophecy names Cyrus. Is it Isaiah naming him 150 years ahead, or a prophet of the 540s naming a king on the march?
b: This is the first time the conqueror of 41:2 and 41:25 is named. Traditional view: Isaiah of Jerusalem, about 700 BC, names Cyrus some 150 years before his time, as a sign that only the LORD foretells the future (44:7–8, 24–26); 1 Kings 13:2 names Josiah centuries in advance, and Josephus says Cyrus read his own name in Isaiah and was moved to free the Jews (Antiquities 11.5–6). Critical view: a prophet among the exiles in the 540s, after Cyrus had begun his conquests, names the king whose victories his hearers were watching, and claims that God planned it and said so. The chapter page sets out both cases.

a: My shepherd!
p: "Shepherd" was a title for kings. God gives a Persian king the title of David. The Greek reads it differently.
b: Mesopotamian kings were called shepherds of their people, and the Bible gives the title to David: "You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2; compare Psalm 78:71). To call a foreign king "my shepherd" was bold, and 45:1 goes further, calling him the LORD's anointed. The Greek translator read the same Hebrew letters as a verb, "who says to Cyrus to be wise" (see the variant). Some scholars propose "my friend" (re'i). The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which links to the shepherd God of 40:11.

a: and to the temple
p: Ezra says Cyrus ordered the temple rebuilt. Its foundation was laid soon after the return; it was finished in 515 BC.
b: Ezra 1:2–4 gives Cyrus's decree: "He has appointed me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah." An Aramaic copy in Ezra 6:3–5 gives its dimensions and orders the cost paid from the royal treasury. "When the builders founded the LORD's temple" (Ezra 3:10), the old men who remembered Solomon's temple wept; work then stalled until 520, and "This house was completed" in 515 (Ezra 6:15). The Cyrus Cylinder, his own proclamation at Babylon, says he returned gods and peoples to their sanctuaries and rebuilt their dwellings; it does not mention Judah, but it shows the same policy.
r: Ezra 1:1–4; Ezra 3:10–13; Ezra 6:3–5; Ezra 6:15; 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Haggai 1:1–8
